title: Low-carbon S30C steel with superior strength and ductility fabricated by powder bed fusion-electron beam
abstract: Abstract This study demonstrates the potential of electron beam powder bed fusion (PBF-EB) for the fabrication of low-carbon S30C steel with superior strength and ductility. In addition to investigating the effect of preheating temperature on microstructural evolution, we examined the effect of subsequent quenching and tempering treatments. At 1033 K, equiaxed α-Fe grains dominated, whereas at 1173 K, elongated grains and side plates aligned with the build direction were more prevalent, resulting in a pronounced < 101 > texture. These microstructural features introduced anisotropy along the build direction, which was effectively mitigated by tempering. Compared with conventionally processed low-carbon S30C steel, the additively manufactured specimens exhibited higher yield and tensile strengths and improved ductility, achieving an ultrahigh tensile strength of 1914 MPa in the as-quenched state, while the as-tempered state exhibited an elongation of ~ 17% with a tensile strength of ~ 886 MPa. The exceptional mechanical performance is attributed to the refined martensitic structures and high dislocation density induced by the PBF-EB process. These findings highlight the capability of PBF-EB to produce structural carbon steels with tunable properties by controlling the process parameters, thereby offering a cost-effective route for the industrial-scale additive manufacturing of steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Steel is an essential structural material in the automotive, construction, and energy industries because of its excellent mechanical properties and cost-effectiveness [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Structural carbon steels can be additively manufactured using powder bed fusion (PBF) because their phase transformation characteristics enable control over strength, toughness, and hardness through heat treatment [ 8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]. Although structural carbon steels exhibit favorable compatibility with PBF in terms of their phase-transformable behavior and thermal processability, several challenges remain in their practical implementation. The use of laser beam-based PBF (PBF-LB) to fabricate carbon steels is challenging because high thermal gradients and rapid solidification induce residual stresses, leading to cracking and brittle fracture [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]. In contrast, the preheated temperature employed during electron beam-based PBF (PBF-EB) suppresses “smoking” and cracking, stabilizes thermal hysteresis, and promotes microstructural uniformity while enabling control over the precipitation and dislocation structures [ 17 ,  18 – 19 ]. Here, powder “smoking” refers to the dispersion/ejection of powder particles from the powder bed during electron-beam irradiation, which destabilizes the powder layer and can interrupt the build process. Preheating mitigates this phenomenon by stabilizing the powder bed and reducing charge accumulation in the irradiated powder layer, thereby improving process robustness. Owing to the affordability and stable supply of carbon steels, PBF–EB is a promising route for producing reliable and high-performance components.

Recent studies have highlighted the unique microstructural features of carbon steels fabricated via PBF-EB. The as-built microstructure of low-carbon S25C steel [ 20 ] was investigated using a substrate preheating temperature of 1158 K and consisted of pearlite with ferrite, cellular regions, and regular and irregular cementite particles. Deformation was mainly localized in irregular cementite, whereas ferrite and regular cementite contributed to plasticity. Similarly, the as-built microstructure of low-carbon S30C steel [ 21 ] was fabricated with a preheating temperature of 1131 K and consisted of ferrite and pearlite. Upon quenching, the structure transformed into fine martensite, which developed into a microstructure with lath martensite, cementite particles, and dislocation networks upon tempering. In addition, a related study on S30C steel [ 22 ] reported that a preheating temperature of approximately 1131 K was required to avoid smoking during PBF-EB. These studies indicate that PBF-EB enables unique pathways for microstructural control, potentially surpassing conventional casting or forging methods.

Preheating suppresses powder “smoking” and prevents crack formation during PBF. Preheating also influences the thermal conditions during fabrication, thereby affecting the formation of the initial microstructure and its subsequent evolution during post-treatments, such as quenching and tempering. Therefore, in this study, we investigated the effects of different preheating temperatures on the microstructure and mechanical properties of low-carbon S30C steel.

sections.heading: Experiments
paragraphs: In this study, gas-atomized powder of low-carbon S30C steel with a nominal composition of Fe–0.3 C–1.0Si–1.0Mn was used; the detailed chemical composition is summarized in Table  1 . The particle size in the powder ranged from 65 to 145 μm. Block specimens with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 35 mm 3  were fabricated on a SUS304 baseplate with dimensions of 150 × 150 × 10 mm 3  using PBF-EB equipment (Arcam A2X, Sweden). The process parameters are summarized in Table  2 . The scan pattern was a raster strategy with bidirectional scanning, and the hatch direction was rotated by 90 degrees between successive layers. The blocks were fabricated in either an upright (vertical) or flat (horizontal) orientation. After fabrication, the as-built specimens (as-B) were heat-treated according to the schedules shown in Fig.  1 : (i) quenching from 1173 K after holding for 900 s (as-Q) followed by water cooling, and (ii) tempering at 873 K for 3600 s (as-QT) followed by water cooling. Conventional hot-rolled S30C steel was used as the reference material. The reference specimens were normalized at 1173 K for 600 s followed by air cooling (as-N-C), and were also quenched and tempered using the same schedule as the as-built specimens (as-QT-C). All the specimens of this study were listed in Table  3 .

The specimens were cut into dog-bone shapes using an electrical discharge machine, as shown in Fig.  2 . Phase analysis was conducted using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, PANalytical X’Pert MPD, Netherlands) with Cu Kα radiation. Microstructural analysis was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Hitachi S-3400 N, Japan) and electron backscatter diffraction (FEI XL30S-FEG, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Tensile tests were conducted at 300 K with an initial strain rate of 1.0 × 10 − 3  s − 1 . Due to limited specimen availability, one tensile specimen was tested for each condition; therefore, the reported tensile properties are representative values.

sections.heading: Phase identification
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows the XRD profiles of the as-B, as-Q, and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K, along with that of the conventional as-N-C specimen. All specimens exhibited the α-Fe phase with a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. The XRD patterns of the as-Q specimens exhibited broader peaks with lower intensities than those of the other specimens, indicating the presence of martensite with significant lattice strain. This result is consistent with the findings of Gui et al. [ 21 ], who also reported broader XRD peaks for the as-Q specimens, indicating high lattice strain in the martensitic structures. In contrast, the XRD patterns of the as-tempered specimens exhibited narrower peaks, indicating a reduction in lattice strain due to the precipitation of carbide (Fe 3 C) from the supersaturated carbon in the α-Fe phase, as observed in similar studies on S30C steel [ 22 ]. The XRD pattern of the conventional as-N-C specimen exhibited the sharpest peaks, indicating minimal lattice strain typical of a stable α-Fe phase.
Fig. 3 XRD patterns of as-B, as-Q, and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K, along with that of conventionally processed as-N-C specimen

sections.heading: Microstructural observation
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the optical images of the top (a and c) and bottom (b and d) regions of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 (a and b) and 1173 K (c and d). In all specimens, the α-Fe phase (white) appears relatively equiaxed in the bottom (b and d) regions. The top regions (a and c) contain elongated/plate-like features, including slanted side plates whose elongation direction is indicated by the red arrows and is approximately parallel to the build direction. These plate-like features are interpreted as transformation-related ferrite (“side plates”) formed during the γ→α transformation, which can develop when the material remains in the γ region for longer and α-Fe grows preferentially along the build direction. The specimen preheated at 1173 K (c and d) exhibited a more pronounced alignment of α-Fe along the build direction and a higher density of side plates than the specimen preheated at 1033 K (a and b). These microstructural features are similar to those reported by Gui et al. [ 21 ] for S30C steel fabricated via PBF-EB. Comparable distributions of equiaxed and columnar grains and directional variations along the build direction were observed in the microstructure. Similar morphological trends have been reported for S25C steel fabricated via PBF-EB [ 20 ]. To support these qualitative observations, we performed a simple image-based quantification on the representative fields shown in Fig.  4  and summarized the results in Table  S1 . Consistent with the more equiaxed appearance of the bottom regions, the equiaxed fraction is higher at the bottom than at the top for both preheating conditions, rising from 68.4% to 84.6% at 1033 K and from 63.5 to 71.6% at 1173 K. Moreover, the top region at 1173 K shows a lower equiaxed fraction than the top region at 1033 K, decreasing from 68.4 to 63.5%, which quantitatively supports the more pronounced presence of elongated and plate-like ferrite features at the higher preheating temperature.

Fig. 4 Optical micrographs of the  a  and  c  top and  b  and  d  bottom regions of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a  and  b  1033 and  c  and  d  1173 K; The red arrows indicate the elongation direction of the plate-like features (side plates)

Figure  5  shows the SEM images of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. The microstructures of both specimens consist of the α-Fe phase and lamellar pearlite with a thickness of approximately 10–50 μm. Figure  6  shows the SEM images of the top and bottom regions of the as-Q specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. Quenching resulted in the formation of needle-shaped lath martensite throughout the specimens, regardless of the position, consistent with the findings of a previous study [ 23 ], which reported that lath martensite typically forms at a carbon content of 0.3 mass%. Figure  7  shows the SEM images of the top and bottom regions of the as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. The lath structure partially collapsed owing to recovery during tempering; however, because martensite barely recrystallized during tempering, its lath morphology was largely retained.

Fig. 5 SEM images of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a – c  1033 and  d – f  1173 K. Panels ( b ) and ( e ) show high-magnification views of ( a ) and ( d ), respectively, and panels ( c ) and ( f ) show high-magnification views of ( b ) and ( e ), respectively
Fig. 6 SEM images of the  a  and  c  top and  b  and  d  bottom regions of the as-Q specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a  and  b  1033 and  c  and  d  1173 K
Fig. 7 SEM images of the  a  and  c  top and  b  and  d  bottom regions of as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a  and  b  1033 and  c  and  d  1173 K

Figure  8  shows the inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of the top and bottom regions of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. The bottom region of the specimen fabricated at 1033 K exhibits a weak crystallographic texture with many randomly oriented α-Fe grains. In contrast, the top region shows a mixed microstructure composed of equiaxed grains, elongated grains aligned along the build direction, and plate-like structures. These plate-like structures are considered side plates because they share the crystallographic orientation of the α-Fe phase and are aligned parallel to the build direction. A weak < 101 > texture is observed in the top region. Equiaxed grains are scarcely observed in the top or bottom regions of the specimen fabricated at a preheating temperature of 1173 K, and the microstructure is dominated by elongated structures aligned along the building direction. The side-plate structures are more pronounced than those in the specimen fabricated at 1033 K, and a distinct < 101 > texture is observed in both regions. Previous studies have reported that S30C steel fabricated via PBF-EB exhibited a weak crystallographic texture [ 20 ], whereas S25C steel showed no clear < 101 > orientation [ 21 ]. In contrast, the S30C specimens fabricated in this study exhibited a clear < 101 > orientation, which became more prominent with increasing preheating temperature. These results indicate that both the preheating temperature and carbon content significantly influence the texture formation in steel fabricated via PBF-EB.
Fig. 8 Inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of the  a  and  c  top and  b  and  d  bottom regions of as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a  and  b  1033 K and  c  and  d  1173 K

Figure  9  shows the IPF maps of the as-Q and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. In the as-Q specimen fabricated at 1173 K, polygonal grains with < 001 > and < 111 > orientations are clearly observed. These grains correspond to prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) formed during the austenitization heat treatment at 1173 K, and they were retained as prior-austenite boundary traces after martensitic transformation on quenching. In contrast, in the IPF map of the specimen fabricated at 1033 K, PAGB traces are also observable; however, they are generally less distinct, and the overall crystallographic texture is weaker. Because both specimens were austenitized at 1173 K prior to quenching, the difference is interpreted mainly as a difference in the apparent visibility/contrast of the PAGB traces rather than the absence of austenite grain boundaries. This difference is attributed to variations in the inherited microstructure and texture introduced during PBF-EB at the lower preheating temperature, which can influence austenite grain growth and variant selection during subsequent austenitization and, consequently, the EBSD contrast of PAGB traces after quenching. The overall texture of both as-QT specimens is further weakened compared with that of the as-Q specimen. Although tempered martensite substructures are observed, packet boundaries and PAGB traces are not clearly visible, likely due to recovery and the resulting reduction of local orientation gradients during tempering. Such polygonal grains and distinct PAGB features were not reported for PBF-fabricated S30C and S25C steels by Gui et al. [ 20 ,  21 ]. These observations suggest that the thermal history during PBF-EB, including the preheating condition, influences the inherited microstructure and texture and thereby affects the prior-austenite grain characteristics formed during austenitization and their apparent retention after quenching and tempering.
Fig. 9 IPF maps of the  a  and  c  as-Q and  b  and  d  as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a  and  b  1033 and  c  and  d  1173 K

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: Table  4  presents the Vickers hardness values for the as-B, as-Q, and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. The as-B specimens exhibited hardness values ranging from 190 to 230 HV, with those preheated at 1173 K exhibiting a higher hardness (230 HV) than those preheated at 1033 K (190 HV). Quenching significantly increased the hardness to approximately 650 HV, whereas subsequent tempering reduced it to approximately 290 HV. No significant differences were observed in the hardness values of the as-Q and as-QT specimens at the two preheating temperatures. Compared with previous studies on PBF-fabricated S30C and S25C steels [ 20 ,  21 ], the as-B specimens in this study exhibited comparable hardness values. In contrast, the quenched specimen preheated at 1173 K exhibited a higher hardness than S30C steel [ 20 ]. These results indicate that the preheating and quenching conditions employed in this study are associated with microstructural refinement, which is consistent with the observed increase in hardness and strength. A statistically robust quantification of the relevant microstructural length scales will be addressed in future work using a broader dataset.

Table 4 Vickers hardness values as-B, as-Q, and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K Condition 1033 K 1173 K as-B 190 ± 2 (HV) 230 ± 2 (HV) as-Q 650 ± 3 (HV) 648 ± 7 (HV) as-QT 288 ± 1 (HV) 293 ± 4 (HV)

Figure  10  shows the tensile stress–strain curves of the as-B, as-Q, and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K, and the corresponding results are summarized in Table  5 . The as-B specimens exhibited similar mechanical properties regardless of the preheating temperature. The as-Q specimen preheated at 1033 K exhibited a higher 0.2% proof stress but lower tensile strength and elongation than the specimen preheated at 1173 K. The as-QT specimen preheated at 1173 K exhibited a slightly higher strength, while its elongation remained nearly the same at both preheating temperatures. Compared with previous studies on PBF-fabricated S30C and S25C steels [ 20 ,  21 ], the as-Q specimen preheated at 1173 K demonstrated significantly greater ductility than S30C steel and a more favorable strength–ductility balance than the extremely strong but brittle S25C steel. These results indicate that the preheating conditions employed in this study improved the mechanical properties through the refined microstructural evolution.
Fig. 10 Tensile stress–strain curves of the as-B, as-Q, and as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K

Figure  11  shows the tensile stress–strain curves for the vertically and horizontally built as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K, and Table  5  summarizes the corresponding results. For comparison, the tensile properties of the as-N-C specimen are shown in Fig.  11  and listed in Table  5 . The as-B specimen preheated at 1033 K exhibited negligible differences between the vertical and horizontal builds, with similar 0.2% proof stress and tensile strength and only approximately 5% lower elongation in the horizontal direction, indicating limited anisotropy. In contrast, the specimen preheated to 1173 K exhibited a more pronounced anisotropy. Compared with the as-N-C specimen, the as-B specimens exhibited a lower 0.2% proof stress of 50 MPa but a higher tensile strength of 20–40 MPa. Figure  12  shows the tensile stress–strain curves for the vertically and horizontally built as-QT specimens fabricated under the same preheating conditions, and Table  5  summarizes the results. For comparison, the tensile properties of the as-QT-C specimen are shown in Fig.  12  and listed in Table  5 . The as-QT specimens exhibited minimal anisotropy, with a difference of only 0.6% in the elongation between the build directions. Furthermore, compared with the as-QT-C specimen, the additively manufactured specimens exhibited an increase of 20–50 MPa in 0.2% proof stress, 40–80 MPa in tensile strength, and 3–4% in elongation.

Figure  13  shows the SEM images of the fracture surfaces of the vertically and horizontally built as-B specimens. Figure  14  shows the SEM images of the as-Q and as-QT specimens. All specimens were fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K. The as-B specimens exhibited both ductile (e.g., dimples) and brittle (e.g., cleavage facets) features. River patterns, which are typically associated with crack propagation during cleavage fractures, are also visible in some regions. The as-Q specimens exhibit intergranular brittle fractures along grain boundaries with distinct facets. Dimples are rarely observed, indicating the dominance of brittle fractures. In contrast, the as-QT specimens exhibit widespread well-formed dimples across the fracture surfaces, indicating a ductile fracture mode. The specimens preheated at 1033 K exhibit deeper and more clearly defined dimples, whereas those preheated at 1173 K exhibit smaller and shallower dimples. These observations indicate that the preheating temperature influenced the morphology of the fracture surface.

Fig. 13 SEM images of the fracture surfaces of  a ,  b ,  e , and  f  vertically and  c ,  d ,  g , and  h  horizontally built as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a – d  1033 and  e – h  1173 K
Fig. 14 SEM images of the fracture surfaces of  a – d  as-Q and  e – h  as-QT specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a ,  b ,  e , and  f  1033 and  c ,  d ,  g , and  h  1173 K

Figure  15  shows the kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of 1033 and 1173 K, along with that of the as-N-C specimen. The as-built specimens exhibited higher local misorientation than the as-N-C specimen, indicating greater plastic strain and higher dislocation density. These high dislocation densities likely contribute to dislocation strengthening, enhancing the yield strength. Consequently, the as-B specimens did not display a distinct upper or lower yield point but instead exhibited continuous yielding behavior.
Fig. 15 KAM maps of the as-B specimens fabricated at preheating temperatures of  a  1033 and  b  1173 K compared with the  c  conventional as-N-C specimen

sections.heading: Effect of preheating temperature on the formation of microstructure
paragraphs: During the PBF-EB process, repeated local melting and solidification occur under EB irradiation. During this process, the steepest temperature gradient is typically established along the build direction, promoting grain growth in that direction. For cubic crystal systems (BCC and FCC), the preferred growth direction is generally < 001> [ 24 ,  25 ]. Accordingly, low-carbon S30C steel initially solidifies as columnar γ-Fe grains oriented along < 001 > in the build direction.

Nevertheless, as shown in the IPF maps in Fig.  8 , the as-B microstructure consists of equiaxed α-Fe grains in the lower region and plate-like side plates near the top region. At a higher preheating temperature of 1173 K, the fraction of equiaxed grains decreased, whereas that of elongated α-Fe grains and side plates aligned with the build direction increased. In contrast, at a lower preheating temperature of 1033 K, the temperature during fabrication lies within the α-phase stability region, resulting in immediate γ→α transformation after solidification. Consequently, the PAGBs and crystallographic orientations were not clearly retained, producing a microstructure with indistinct grain boundaries. The specimen preheated to 1173 K exhibited a strong < 101 > texture along the building direction. This texture is attributed to the phase change from γ-Fe to α-Fe during cooling. At 1173 K, the material remains in the γ-Fe single-phase region during the build, allowing γ-Fe to persist until cooling begins. Upon cooling, α-Fe first precipitates along the grain boundaries of the columnar γ-Fe grains. Because these boundaries are aligned with the build direction, the newly formed α-Fe also grows in the same direction.

Figure  16  shows a schematic of the microstructural evolution of the specimen preheated at 1173 K, highlighting grain elongation along the build direction and the development of an enhanced {110}-type texture component in α-Fe. As previously noted, the γ-Fe phase formed during initial solidification has a < 001 > orientation along the build direction. Upon cooling, this γ-Fe transforms into α-Fe following a Kurdjumov–Sachs (K–S) type orientation relationship.
Fig. 16 Schematic of ferrite growth along the build direction and the development of a strong < 101 > texture in S30C steel fabricated via PBF-EB

However, the opposite side of the boundary with the other γ-Fe grain can be less coherent. Such grain boundary allotriomorphic α is known to grow preferentially into the adjacent γ-Fe grain where the interfacial condition is less favorable (i.e., not maintaining the same low-misfit relationship) [ 7 ,  28 ]. Importantly, the K–S relationship permits multiple symmetry-related α variants for a given γ orientation; therefore, a specific α direction parallel to BD is not uniquely determined by γ < 001>//BD. Instead, under the directional thermal history in PBF-EB, variant selection can occur, and variants that are favorable for growth along BD and/or for reducing interfacial energy may be preferentially formed, leading to an apparent enhancement of the {110}-type intensity along BD. As cooling progresses and undercooling increases, plate-like α-Fe structures known as side plates begin to grow within the γ-Fe grains. These side plates also follow a K–S type orientation relationship [ 25 ] and, together with the grain boundary allotriomorphs, can contribute to the enhanced {110}-type texture component. This transformation sequence highlights the role of interfacial crystallography and the directional thermal history in determining the final texture of S30C steel fabricated via PBF-EB.

sections.heading: Differences in mechanical properties due to preheating temperature, anisotropy, and effects of heat treatment
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  11 , the specimen preheated at 1033 K exhibited minimal differences in mechanical properties between the vertically and horizontally built specimens. In contrast, the specimen preheated at 1173 K exhibited pronounced anisotropy in elongation, with higher and lower ductility in the vertical and horizontal directions, respectively. This anisotropy is attributed to the elongated α-Fe grains and side plate structures with a strong < 101 > crystallographic texture along the build direction, which suppresses the activation of specific slip systems in a direction-dependent manner and reduces plastic deformability, particularly in the horizontal direction [ 29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ]. The tempering treatment significantly reduced the anisotropy, as shown in Fig.  12 , with the difference in elongation between the build directions narrowing to only 0.6%. This reduction is attributed to the recrystallization and recovery processes occurring at the PAGBs and packet boundaries during quenching and tempering. These processes likely weakened the texture and contributed to microstructural homogenization, thereby mitigating the direction-dependent mechanical behavior.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, we examined the effects of preheating temperature and subsequent heat treatments on the microstructural and mechanical properties of low-carbon S30C steel fabricated via PBF-EB. Preheating at 1173 K promoted the alignment of elongated ferrite grains and side-plate structures with the build direction, producing a pronounced < 101 > texture and ductility anisotropy. In contrast, preheating at 1033 K resulted in more equiaxed grains and reduced anisotropy. Quenching generated fine lath martensite with high hardness and strength, whereas tempering effectively reduced anisotropy and improved ductility. The as-Q specimens achieved an ultrahigh tensile strength of more than 1900 MPa, whereas the as-QT specimens exhibited a superior strength–ductility balance with a tensile strength of approximately 850–900 MPa and an elongation of approximately 17%.

These findings demonstrate that the thermal history during PBF-EB processing plays a decisive role in microstructural evolution and texture development. Optimizing preheating and heat treatment conditions enables the fabrication of structural carbon steels with tailored properties, supporting reliable and cost-effective industrial applications of additive manufacturing of steel.
